title: Stat 3125 ProjectGuide
text:
This website exists as a resource for STAT 3125 students looking to create a semester project with the intention of presenting at Analytics Day, fulfilling an honors contract, or simply expanding their portfolio.
Resources available on this site include but are not limited to:

Where to find your dataset
Using popular R packages to make data analysis easier
Performing Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
Possible data processing/modeling methods
Using ggplot2 for easy plot creation
Assembling a presentation/poster

If this is your first time using the site, it is recommended to begin by reading our Getting Started page, which will prepare you for your upcoming project.

title: Getting Started
text:
Before a student can get underway with a project, there are a few pieces of prerequisite knowledge that are recommended to prevent roadblocks further down the line.

R and R Studio: The first couple weeks of class will ensure that you are set up with this software, as it is required for classwork. The guides on this website are written with R users in mind.
Popular R packages: These packages will make appearances in some of the example projects on this site and greatly simplify the work of data analysis and visualization.

title: Example Project A: Identifying Opioid Misuse Indicators Among Rural Populations
Example Project B: Using Differentials in GLM-Predicted Success to Analyze Opioid Rehabilitation Treatment Decisions
text:
This article documents yet another example project made by an undergraduate student at KSU.

Finding a Dataset
At the beginning of the semester, the student approached their professor inquiring about the possibility of doing a research project in parallel with their classwork as a part of an honors contract. The professor referred the student to the Treatment Episode Data Set (TEDS), a nationwide yearly report on all recorded instances of formal treatment for substance abuse in the United States.


Choosing a Question
When reading over the dataset, the student noticed a variable, METHUSE, which denoted whether the patient was given opioid therapy[footnote on definition here] or not. Seeing this flag, the student wondered how patients already struggling with addiction to opioids would fare in their outcome when given or not given opioid therapy. The dataset contained another variable, REASON, which denoted the final result of the patient’s treatment, such as completing rehab, dropping out, or being kicked out. Using these variables, the student formulated their question:

“Among patients in treatment for opioid addiction, does prescribing opioid therapy have a positive or negative impact on outcome?”



Performing Exploratory Data Analysis
With a question in mind, the student moved onto the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) step of their project. To quantify the efficacy of opioid therapy, they created a binary variable SUCCESS as a logical filter of REASON. The table below demonstrates the assignment of SUCCESS:

Although it was possible that opioid therapy was having a strong negative impact on patient outcomes, the student suspected that situational factors would lead to a strong correlation between patients having more difficult (less likely to be successful) cases and requiring opioid therapy. This hypothesis led the student to decide how they wanted to model their data.


Modeling Data
To isolate for situation, the student chose to train a generalized linear model (GLM) on every opioid patient’s situational factors upon their arrival to treatment, such as:

Filtering Factors (requirements to be in study, e.g. primary substance)
Demographic Factors (age, race, sex, etc.)
Drug Usage Factors (frequency/route of use, age at first use)

to estimate their likelihood of successful rehabilitation when they arrive at the institution. With each patient assigned a predicted success value, the residual of their actual vs. predicted success would provide, in the aggregate, a picture of what treatment decisions are better or worse for patients.


Analyzing Results
With residuals calculated, the final step was to group patients and calculate their aggregate response to opioid therapy to see where the practice is most and least effective. One such visual derived from the analysis phase of this project is the radar plot below, which groups by the SERVICES setting the patient was in upon arrival.



Creating a Report
With multiple rounds of results analysis complete, the final step for the student was to compile their findings into a report. Since the student wanted to present their project at KSU analytics day at the end of the semester, they used a template from the analytics day website to structure their report in a poster board format. They condensed their background, methods, results, and conclusions into paragraph format and added their relevant visuals, and their project was done!
The full report has been attached below for future reference.

title: An Introduction to finalfit
text:
Introduction
For Project A, The student utilized the finalfit package to create clean tables for their logistic regression model. finalfit is an open-source package to be used with R Studio to create clean, publication-ready tables for the data analysis model of your choosing. The package compiles your numbers into a table, grouping data in an efficient, automated way to present in a paper or poster. finalfit is a great programming package for beginners in data analytics research.


Use Cases and Limitations



finalfit Can:

Summarize quantitative variable values by a categorical variable
Summarize regression model results in table format
Summarize regression model results into a plot






finalfit Cannot:

Analyze results from advanced machine learning models
Handle large amounts of levels for categorical variables
Perform Bayesian modeling

title: Choosing Your Question
text: When choosing your research question, it’s important to look at all your different variables and determine what you would like to assess. Pick something that is meaningful to you, you can connect with, or something that genuinely interests you. When I first started this project, I scrolled through the dataset and looked at all the different variables and numbers. There’s many to choose from, so you’ll want to narrow it down significantly. Try not to get overwhelmed and lost in all the numbers – take this time to gather ideas. Upon looking through the dataset, I thought about what I might want to investigate or what story I want to tell. I have an interest in healthcare deserts and mental health, so it made sense to look at opioid misuse in rural populations in people with and without mental health disorders. I was able to further narrow this down to looking at young adults in the south as my sample. This decision allowed for me to have more connection with this analysis as I could fall into these categories based on my age and where I live. Overall, the important thing to remember when choosing your question is to think about the story you want to tell using the data you are given.

title: An Introduction to dplyr
text:
Introduction
Per its website, dplyr is “a grammar of data manipulation” that greatly simplifies data processing using core verbiage such as:

group_by(): subdivides datasets for independent analysis
filter(): removes values that do not match a given condition
mutate(): creates new variables from existing ones
summarize(): aggregates data from multiple values into a single summary value
select(): selects (or deselects) variables to include or exclude from the dataset



Improvements over base R
While dplyr’s data manipulation features do not enable the user to perform any actions that aren’t possible in base R, its simplicity is its key. dplyr allows users to transform their datasets in simple commands rather than nested function calls. The following table from the official dplyr <-> base R article demonstrates the reduction in complexity that dplyr functions enable.







dplyr
base




arrange(df, x)
df[order(x), , drop = FALSE]


distinct(df, x)
df[!duplicated(x), , drop = FALSE], unique()


filter(df, x)
df[which(x), , drop = FALSE], subset()


mutate(df, z = x + y)
df$z <- df$x + df$y, transform()


pull(df, 1)
df[[1]]


pull(df, x)
df$x


rename(df, y = x)
names(df)[names(df) == "x"] <- "y"


relocate(df, y)
df[union("y", names(df))]


select(df, x, y)
df[c("x", "y")], subset()


select(df, starts_with("x"))
df[grep("^x", names(df))]


summarise(df, mean(x))
mean(df$x), tapply(), aggregate(), by()


slice(df, c(1, 2, 5))
df[c(1, 2, 5), , drop = FALSE]



In addition to reducing individual calls, some dplyr functions would require multiple separate calls in base R to achieve the same result. For example, let’s examine the iris dataset, a staple resource in data science education, and attempt to tally the number of flowers of each species in the dataset. In dplyr, all we would have to do is:

library(dplyr)
data <- iris %>%
group_by(Species) %>%
summarize(mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width)) %>%
print()

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Species    mean_sepal_width
  <fct>                 <dbl>
1 setosa                 3.43
2 versicolor             2.77
3 virginica              2.97


The equivalent code in base R would look something like this:

means <- tapply(iris$Sepal.Width, iris$Species, mean)
data <- data.frame(
  Species = names(means),
  mean_sepal_width = as.vector(means),
  row.names = NULL
)
print(data)

     Species mean_sepal_width
1     setosa            3.428
2 versicolor            2.770
3  virginica            2.974


Note how dplyr avoids repeat references as well as intermediary variables. These are some of the many reasons data scientists prefer dplyr for R data manipulation.


A Note on Pipes in R
If characters such as %>% or |> look unfamiliar to you, that may be because you’ve never worked with R’s pipe system before. Put simply, pipes are simple operators that allow programmers to chain functions to each other using common data, reducing redundant object references and simplifying code.
For example, let’s look at the code below (once again using the iris dataset), where the user is attempting to calculate how the average sepal width of setosa and versicolor flowers compare.

Base Code

library(dplyr)
data <- iris
data <- filter(data, Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor"))
data <- group_by(data, Species)
data <- summarize(data, mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width))
print(data)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Species    mean_sepal_width
  <fct>                 <dbl>
1 setosa                 3.43
2 versicolor             2.77




Using Pipes

library(dplyr)
data <- iris %>%
  filter(Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor")) %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarize(mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width)) %>%
  print()

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Species    mean_sepal_width
  <fct>                 <dbl>
1 setosa                 3.43
2 versicolor             2.77


When you use pipes, the object and its variables are preserved between operations, making references much more intuitive and code less cluttered. It can take a bit to adjust, but once you get comfortable using pipes it will make your R coding much easier.



Learn More
If you would like to learn more about dplyr, visit its website for more information.

title: Formulating a Research Question
text:
When developing a research question, it is essential to systematically examine the available variables to determine exactly what needs to be assessed. Selecting a topic that aligns with personal interests or real-world experiences can significantly enhance a researcher’s engagement and final analysis.
Initially, exploring a large dataset can feel overwhelming due to the sheer volume of numbers and variables. However, this preliminary phase is best used for brainstorming and identifying potential data stories rather than getting lost in the figures. To produce a manageable and impactful analysis, the broad scope must eventually be narrowed down significantly.






NoteCase Study: From Broad Concept to Specific Sample



Consider a researcher who has an interest in healthcare deserts and mental health. Rather than attempting to analyze an entire multi-faceted dataset, they might choose to look specifically at opioid misuse in rural populations, comparing individuals with and without mental health disorders.
To refine the scope even further, the researcher could limit their sample to young adults in the American South. Aligning the research parameters with a demographic or geographic region that the researcher understands intimately adds valuable context, insight, and personal connection to the study.


Ultimately, the most important element of choosing a research question is identifying the core narrative that the data is uniquely equipped to tell.

title: Finding a Dataset
text:
The first step in developing a project in data science is finding a dataset to analyze. Students may pursue a variety of avenues when sourcing their data, and the below sections serve to highlight some of the most popular and extensive free data hubs on the internet.

Data.gov
Data.gov is the US government’s central host for public data, containing over 500,000 datasets as of 2026. Most relevant to Stat 3125 students, the site hosts nearly 20,000 datasets from the Department of Health & Human Services, with most popular datasets including:

U.S. Chronic Disease Indicators (Last updated 6/4/2026)
NCHS - Leading Causes of Death: United States (Last updated 4/21/2025)
Mental Health Care in the Last 4 Weeks (Last updated 4/21/2025)

In addition, the Center for Disease Control (CDC) hosts its own portal for open data, available at data.cdc.gov. The site hosts over 1,500 datasets, including many key data sources covering the COVID-19 pandemic.


Kaggle
Kaggle is a privately-run platform for datasets and data science competitions. Users are free to publish their own data sets and respond to others with their own analysis. Nearly any topic of dataset can be found on Kaggle, from sports to disease to animal species. The key drawback of Kaggle is that the public nature of its data can make it difficult to find quality datasets at times.


Google Dataset Search
Google Dataset Search is a search tool built on the foundations of Google Research that aggregates public datasets from across the internet into a searchable site. Details included in searches include:

Data source
Data format
Date last updated
Description
Governing body (when applicable)

Google Dataset Search is a good resource for students who know the topic they want to cover but want a wholistic picture of possible data sources.

title: Performing Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Once you have acquired a dataset to study, the first step in the analytical process is exploratory data analysis, or EDA. EDA is the process of observing and summarizing the key characteristics of a dataset to uncover basic underlying trends before diving deeper into advanced analysis. The exact steps of EDA that fit a project best will vary based on the dataset you’re studying, but this article will lay out some of the paths you can take during this step of your analytical process.

Descriptive Statistics
Descriptive statistics are basic measurements of dimension and spread that can give the user an understanding of the expected ranges and centers of a dataset’s variables. The psych package in R contains a function describe() which is quite effective for generating a litany of descriptive statistics, as shown in the example below:

library(psych)
describe(iris)

             vars   n mean   sd median trimmed  mad min max range  skew
Sepal.Length    1 150 5.84 0.83   5.80    5.81 1.04 4.3 7.9   3.6  0.31
Sepal.Width     2 150 3.06 0.44   3.00    3.04 0.44 2.0 4.4   2.4  0.31
Petal.Length    3 150 3.76 1.77   4.35    3.76 1.85 1.0 6.9   5.9 -0.27
Petal.Width     4 150 1.20 0.76   1.30    1.18 1.04 0.1 2.5   2.4 -0.10
Species*        5 150 2.00 0.82   2.00    2.00 1.48 1.0 3.0   2.0  0.00
             kurtosis   se
Sepal.Length    -0.61 0.07
Sepal.Width      0.14 0.04
Petal.Length    -1.42 0.14
Petal.Width     -1.36 0.06
Species*        -1.52 0.07




Univariate Analysis
It helps to have descriptive statistics of a dataset, but if you want to get a better look at a single variable you may want to perform univariate analysis and visualize it. Regardless of whether the variable in question is quantitative or categorical, multiple avenues of univariate analysis lay at your disposal.

Categorical Univariate Analysis

Frequency Tables (Absolute and Relative)

A simple method to display the number of appearances of each option within a chosen variable. Ex:

# Absolute Frequency Table
table(iris$Species)


    setosa versicolor  virginica 
        50         50         50 

# Relative Frequency table
prop.table(table(iris$Species))


    setosa versicolor  virginica 
 0.3333333  0.3333333  0.3333333 



Pie Charts & Bar Charts

Two simple plots to visually describe the characteristics of quantitative variables. Bar charts are more modular and easier to create in ggplot2 whereas pie charts are generally more visually appealing to general audiences. Ex:

library(ggplot2)
# Bar Chart
ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Species)) +
geom_bar(aes(fill = Species)) +
theme_minimal()







# Pie Chart
ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = "", fill = Species)) +
geom_bar(color = "white", width = 1) +
coord_polar(theta = "y", start = 0) +
theme_minimal() +
labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)










Quantitative Univariate Analysis

Histograms

Charts that show the distribution of a variable in fine detail, consolidating points into small “bins” on the X axis and tallying the number of observations that fall into each bin on the Y axis. Ex:

# Histogram
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Petal.Length)) +
geom_histogram() +
theme_minimal()









Box Plots

Charts that visualize the general spread of an object in the form of key characteristics, including:
a. Expected Minimums/Maximums (outer ticks)
b. Q1 and Q3 indicators (box width)
c. Median (middle dash in box)
d. Outliers (dots outside outer ticks)

# Box Plot
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Petal.Length)) +
geom_boxplot() +
theme_minimal()










Footnote
All the following charts can be used in multivariate analysis as well through the addition of another variable as the fill factor (except the pie chart). Let’s use the histogram from earlier as example to highlight how this added layer of complexity can reveal more about a dataset’s underlying trends:

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, fill = Species)) +
geom_histogram() +
theme_minimal()











Bivariate Analysis

Bivariate Analysis - 2 Categorical Variables

Contingency Tables

Tables that tally the number of entries in a dataset that have each possible value across two or more variables. For our example, we will use a contingency table on mtcars, another example dataset from R, to count the number of cars with x cylinders and y carburetors.

table(
    as.factor(mtcars$cyl),
    as.factor(mtcars$carb),
    dnn=c("Cylinders", "Carburetors"))

         Carburetors
Cylinders 1 2 3 4 6 8
        4 5 6 0 0 0 0
        6 2 0 0 4 1 0
        8 0 4 3 6 0 1


Note: although the variables cyl and carb are technically numerical, we can use as.factor() to cast them to a categorical form, which can be helpful for numerical variables that behave categorically (such as cylinders in a car engine)
We can add a third variable to this tabulation as well, which will create a table for each of its values. In this example, we use am, which denotes whether a car has automatic (0) or manual (1) transmission.

table(
    as.factor(mtcars$cyl),
    as.factor(mtcars$carb),
    as.factor(mtcars$am),
    dnn=c("Cylinders", "Carburetors", "isManual"))

, , isManual = 0

         Carburetors
Cylinders 1 2 3 4 6 8
        4 1 2 0 0 0 0
        6 2 0 0 2 0 0
        8 0 4 3 5 0 0

, , isManual = 1

         Carburetors
Cylinders 1 2 3 4 6 8
        4 4 4 0 0 0 0
        6 0 0 0 2 1 0
        8 0 0 0 1 0 1


If it is more valuable to have these values as a representation of a percentage of a group, we can make these tables proportional using the prop.table() method. However, the group used as reference for determining each cell’s proportion depends on the value chosen for margin.

margin = 1: Proportional across rows (row sums = 100%)
margin = 2: Proportional across columns (column sums = 100%)
margin = NA: Proportional across all values (sum of all cells = 100%)

Let’s see this in action with mtcars one more time, making a table along each margin value.

#Proportional Across Rows
prop.table(
    table(
        as.factor(mtcars$cyl),
        as.factor(mtcars$carb),
        dnn=c("Cylinders", "Carburetors")),
    margin = 1
)

         Carburetors
Cylinders          1          2          3          4          6          8
        4 0.45454545 0.54545455 0.00000000 0.00000000 0.00000000 0.00000000
        6 0.28571429 0.00000000 0.00000000 0.57142857 0.14285714 0.00000000
        8 0.00000000 0.28571429 0.21428571 0.42857143 0.00000000 0.07142857

#Proportional Across Columns
prop.table(
    table(
        as.factor(mtcars$cyl),
        as.factor(mtcars$carb),
        dnn=c("Cylinders", "Carburetors")),
    margin = 2
)

         Carburetors
Cylinders         1         2         3         4         6         8
        4 0.7142857 0.6000000 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000
        6 0.2857143 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.4000000 1.0000000 0.0000000
        8 0.0000000 0.4000000 1.0000000 0.6000000 0.0000000 1.0000000

#Proportional Across All Values
prop.table(
    table(
        as.factor(mtcars$cyl),
        as.factor(mtcars$carb),
        dnn=c("Cylinders", "Carburetors"))
)

         Carburetors
Cylinders       1       2       3       4       6       8
        4 0.15625 0.18750 0.00000 0.00000 0.00000 0.00000
        6 0.06250 0.00000 0.00000 0.12500 0.03125 0.00000
        8 0.00000 0.12500 0.09375 0.18750 0.00000 0.03125


These proportional values make it very easy to begin to analyze the behavior of these categorical variables. For example, in mtcars:

All 4-cylinder cars have only 1 or 2 carburetors.
71% of cars with 1 carburetor only have 4 cylinders.
The two most common types of cars by cylinder and carburetor count are 4cyl-2carb and 8cyl-4carb, at 18.75% total proportion each.


Chi-Square Test of Independence

If you want to test the relationship between two categorical variables, you can perform a Chi-Square test to evaluate their independence. For example, let’s use the HairEyeColor dataset and test if hair and eye color are related.

library(tidyr)
#Initial dataset contains tallies, revert to observations with uncount()
data <- as.data.frame(HairEyeColor) |>
  uncount(Freq)

#Data must be in table format for test
hair_eye_table <- table(data$Hair, data$Eye)

results <- chisq.test(hair_eye_table)
print(results)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  hair_eye_table
X-squared = 138.29, df = 9, p-value < 2.2e-16


Each of the output values from the test have their own importance, but what we care about most is the p-value, which can be interpreted as such:

If there were no relationship between hair color and eye color in the overall population, the probability that their relationship would randomly appear as it does in this sample (p) is 2.2 * 10-16. Since p < 0.05, we can state that the result is statistically significant and reject the null hypothesis, H0, that there is no relationship between hair and eye color.

If you would like to learn more about performing chi-square tests in R, we recommend this article for further reading.


Multivariate Analysis - 2 or More Quantitative Variables

Scatter Plot

Scatter plots are the simplest form of quantitative multivariate analysis, and can be transformed to add detail in many ways. In ggplot, attributes such as size and color can be assigned to a dataset’s variables to express information in a digestible manner.
Below are two examples of themes within iris and mtcars visualized using scatter plots.

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Sepal.Width, y = Sepal.Length,
size = Petal.Length, color = Species)) +
geom_point() +
labs(
    title = "Sepal and Petal Size by Species",
    subtitle = "Data = iris, n = 150"
) +
theme_minimal()









library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg,
size = cyl, color = as.factor(vs))) +
geom_point() +
labs(
    title = "Scatter Plot of MPG by horsepower",
    subtitle = "Data = mtcars, n = 32",
    color = "EngineIsStraight",
    size = "Cylinders",
    x = "Horsepower",
    y = "Miles Per Gallon (MPG)"
) +
theme_minimal()









Density Plot

Density plots are the two-dimensional equivalent of histograms, with counts expressed on a color scale since the Y-axis is no longer available. If you make a scatter plot of your dataset, but there are too many points to discern any valuable information, there are two best options: Reduce the alpha value, which controls opacity, in the aes field, or replace the scatter plot with a density plot.
The following example shows the strength of making a density plot when analyzing a large dataset, such as diamonds.

library(ggplot2)
data(diamonds)
diamonds |>
  ggplot(aes(x = carat, y = price)) + 
  geom_hex(bins = 70) +
  # Uses transform = "sqrt" for a gentler compression curve
  scale_fill_viridis_c(transform = "sqrt") +
  labs(
    title = "Heatmap of Diamond Price by Carat",
    subtitle = "Data = diamonds, n = 53940",
    x = "Carats",
    y = "Price (USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Line Plot

For ordinal data, especially time-based variables, line plots can visualize trends in a highly digestible manner.
The following example uses the nycflights13 package for acquisition and the lubridate package, an all-in-one tool for date and time manipulation, for transformation.

library(nycflights13)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)

flights |>
  # Floor the date to the beginning of the week
  mutate(date = floor_date(time_hour, unit = "week")) |>
  # Exclude partial weeks
  filter(date > as_date("2012-12-30") & date < as_date("2013-12-29")) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarize(n_flights = n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = n_flights)) +
  geom_line() +
  # Reformat X-axis for readability
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "2 months") +
  labs(
    title = "2013 Total Flights per Week",
    subtitle = "Incomplete weeks omitted for visual clarity",
    y = "count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Correlograms

Correlograms are plots that show the correlation value between all quantitative variables in a dataset. They can easily present a variety of leads that you could investigate as you build your hypothesis. Ex:

library(GGally)
library(ggplot2)

ggcorr(mtcars, 
       method = c("everything", "pearson"),
       label = TRUE,
       label_size = 3,
       label_round = 2 
       ) +
  labs(title = "mtcars Variable Correlogram") +
  theme_minimal()








This plot immediately presents a variety of leads, such as:

As cylinders, displacement, horsepower, and weight increase, MPG tends to decrease.
Manual cars have a strong positive correlation with gear count
Carburetor count has a strong positive correlation with horsepower




Conclusion
When performing EDA during project development, you likely won’t need to use all these methods. There is a skill to understanding which process best fits your dataset, and that will come with time. When preparing to perform EDA, ask yourself:

What variables appear most important? Are they categorical or quantitative?
What variable relationships will define my study? How can I frame them initially?
What findings from EDA would provide valuable context to my audience and are worth using in the final report?

If you can come up with well-thought-out answers to questions like these, EDA will become much easier.
